extracted.intended_audience: naturalists, ornithologists, students and readers of evolutionary biology / natural history
extracted.subtask_description: Interpreting rules and cases by which adult and immature plumage, and sexual differences in colour and ornament, arise and are transmitted in birds — including relations to nidification, seasonal moulting, age-limited inheritance, and sexual selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wallace's nidification rule (female conspicuousness correlates with concealed nests)
rubrics_metrics.description: A large majority of species in which the females are conspicuously coloured (and usually the males also) build concealed or domed nests, presumably gaining protection from their manner of nidification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wallace enumerates many groups (examples: kingfishers, toucans, trogons, puff-birds, plantain-eaters, woodpeckers, parrots) as fitting this rule. Use as supporting evidence for hypotheses that bright female coloration can be retained where nesting provides protection. Note: Darwin accepts many instances but also discusses exceptions and alternative causal directions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Darwin's alternative causal ordering (colour first, nidification second)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where females have become bright (by partaking of male colour via inheritance), they may subsequently change their nesting instincts — seeking more concealed or domed nests to gain protection for conspicuous females.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin argues it is often more probable that females first acquired bright colours (via sexual selection/transmission) and were then led to modify nesting habits (by change of instinct or natural selection acting on spontaneous variations in nesting). Evidence adduced includes geographic and species-level nest differences and cases where nesting habits vary within species or regions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lack of a universal relation between female colour and nest type
rubrics_metrics.description: There is not a close and general relation across all birds between the conspicuousness of the female and whether the nest is concealed; many counterexamples exist within British and other avifaunas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin lists many British species that build in holes or domed nests yet have inconspicuous females, and vice versa. Use such counterexamples to test the generality of any proposed rule; do not overgeneralize from particular groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limited transmission of male-acquired variations to females
rubrics_metrics.description: Sexual differences may often be explained by variations acquired by males through sexual selection being from the first limited in transmission to females, rather than by natural selection removing female variants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin emphasizes the complexity and apparent capriciousness of inheritance laws; degree of limitation can differ between related species and explains graduated differences. Examples: slight female differences in groups where sexes generally alike (kingfishers, parrots, pigeons).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inheritance at corresponding ages / immature plumage reflects ancestral condition
rubrics_metrics.description: When adults differ in colour from the young, and juvenile colours are not evidently adaptive, juvenile plumage often represents a retained ancestral character; immature plumage of several species resembling each other supports this view.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use resemblance among juveniles of allied species as evidence that the ancestor had that plumage. Examples: stripes/spots in young gallinaceous birds, striped young of pigs/tapir, spotted and mottled patterns in thrushes and buntings. This principle underlies many inferences about ancestral states.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seasonal plumage / double moult origin (practical function before sexual display)
rubrics_metrics.description: The habit of moulting twice yearly was probably first acquired for a distinct practical purpose (e.g., acquiring a warmer winter covering) rather than solely to shed sexual ornaments; summer ornamental plumage may then be accumulated by sexual selection at the season when it is retained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin argues against the generality of the idea that double moult evolved primarily to remove dangerous ornaments in winter — cites counterexamples (Birds of Paradise, Argus pheasant, peacock) that do not cast plumes, and species like ptarmigan moulting 3 times. Consider ecological/thermoregulatory explanations first; sexual selection may act on seasonal plumage once seasonality exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish pathological or abnormal masculine traits from inheritance-driven changes
rubrics_metrics.description: Cases where females abnormally or pathologically assume male characters, or where young fertile females temporarily show male traits, should not be conflated with inheritance-at-ages phenomena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin warns to separate diseased/old females or early-acquiring females (via variation/unknown causes) from cases where females acquire male-like traits later in life through normal inheritance patterns. Examples cited (Lanius, Ruticilla, Linaria, Anas, Pyranga aestiva). Treat abnormal cases as anti-patterns when inferring evolutionary rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sexual differences within groups resemble interspecific differences (supporting sexual selection)
rubrics_metrics.description: The nature of sexual differences between the sexes within species is generally of the same kind as the differences between distinct species of the same group, suggesting both arise from similar causes — notably sexual selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin uses this similarity to argue that sexual selection is a major cause of male ornamentation and that the same kinds of colour/pattern elements are involved both intra- and interspecifically. Use pattern similarity across sexes and species as supporting evidence for sexual-selection-driven change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Six rules/classes for relation of juvenile and adult plumage (I–VI)
rubrics_metrics.description: A taxonomy of cases describing how juveniles relate to adult male and female plumage: I) when adult male more beautiful, juveniles resemble adult female; II) when adult female more conspicuous, juveniles resemble adult male; III) when adults alike, juveniles have a peculiar first plumage; IV) when adults alike, juveniles resemble adults; V) when adults have seasonal plumages, juveniles usually resemble adults in winter dress (or intermediate); VI) in some cases juveniles differ by sex, males resembling adult males and females adult females.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin frames these as general rules that graduate into one another; to apply them, examine comparative data across allied species and seasonal forms. He tabulated facts from major regional bird works (Macgillivray, Audubon, Jerdon, Gould) to assess prevalence. Use these six classes as an organizing rubric when categorizing species' ontogenetic plumage patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Class I elaboration: young resemble adult female when male modified
rubrics_metrics.description: When the adult male differs conspicuously from the adult female, the young of both sexes in their first plumage commonly resemble the adult female; this supports the inference that males alone have been modified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin gives many examples (pheasant, duck, house-sparrow) and notes gradations and transitional cases. He cites additional evidence from closely-allied representative species across regions where males differ but females and young remain indistinguishable, supporting male-specific modification. Use comparison among representative species to test whether male traits are derived.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variability of sex-difference transmission within genera/families
rubrics_metrics.description: Within the same family or genus, some species may have sexes identically alike while others are widely dissimilar; the form of transmission (whether characters are expressed in one or both sexes) can vary markedly even among closely-related species.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include sparrows, fly-catchers, thrushes, grouse, pheasants, pigeons; domestic breeds (fowl vs pigeon) show analogous variability. Expect heterogeneity in inheritance patterns across related taxa; do not assume uniform sex-limited transmission within a genus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of geographic and ontogenetic data for inference (representative species comparison)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comparing adult males, females, and young across closely-allied, geographically separated (representative) species can reveal which sex has been modified — e.g., adult males differ while females and young remain alike across regions indicates male modification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin cites Mr. Blyth's observations and examples (Thamnobia, Nectarinia, Tephrodornis, some kingfishers and pheasants). Employ geographic replication and compare immature/plumage states to infer directionality of change.
